title: Sensor Coverage Comparison
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Robotics and Computational Thinking
description: A top-down view of the robot that compares the range, beam width, and blind spots of the ToF, ultrasonic, IR, and bump sensors as students drag an obstacle around.

educational.topic: Comparing robot distance and contact sensors
learningObjectives: Compare the range, beam width, and minimum range of the ToF, ultrasonic, IR, and bump sensors.
Identify blind spots where no sensor detects an obstacle.
Explain which materials fool which sensors (glass and ToF, soft cloth and ultrasonic).
Choose a combination of sensors that covers a given robot task.
prerequisites: ToF, ultrasonic, IR, and bump switch sections (Chapter 8)
Driving forward and stopping with PWM motor control (Chapter 7)
Reading angles and distances on a diagram

controls.label: Obstacle
controls.purpose: Drag the obstacle anywhere in the play area.

controls.label: ToF, Ultrasonic, IR, Bump
controls.purpose: Turn each sensor on or off.

controls.label: Obstacle
controls.purpose: Change what the obstacle is made of.

controls.label: Drive forward
controls.purpose: Drive at 10 cm per second until the bump switch touches the obstacle.

controls.label: Zoom in near robot
controls.purpose: Switch from 2 px per cm (about 200 cm deep) to 6 px per cm (about 60 cm deep).

equations: IR: two 2 cm wide strips reaching 10 cm from the front corners
Bump: contact with the front edge
detected if the obstacle circle overlaps the zone and is not closer than the minimum range
assumptions: Glass is invisible to the ToF laser; soft cloth is invisible to the ultrasonic sensor.
Readings are the distance from the sensor to the nearest edge of the obstacle.
limitations: Real beams have soft edges and shorter ranges for small, dark, or angled targets.
Bright light and surface texture are not modeled.

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Comparison through exploration and a design task
pedagogical.interactionPattern: Drag-to-explore coverage map with lit zones, a readings legend, and a drive-forward test
keyQuestions: Which sensor sees farthest, and which sees widest?
Where are the blind spots around the robot?
Which sensors would you combine to avoid glass doors and soft furniture?
commonMisconceptions: One distance sensor can see everything around the robot.
A sensor can measure an obstacle that is touching it.
assessmentOpportunities: Find the sensor that notices an obstacle just ahead of the left front corner.
Find the sensor that still works when the obstacle is glass at 50 cm.
Choose and justify a sensor combination for a given task.
